h1: The 8 Best 36V Leaf Blowers of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 cordless leaf blowers in the 36V class compared on airflow, battery platform, weight and kit contents, from Makita to EGO.
summary: The Makita XBU02PT is the best 36V-class kit here: two 18V batteries make 36V, a brushless motor, 473 CFM and the charger in the box. For maximum force, the EGO Power+ listing at 880 CFM is the airflow champion. If you already own Makita batteries, the bare XBU02Z saves money. Two picks, the Milwaukee M18 and the Makita XBU03Z, are single-18V tools, so they sit at the edge of this category.
intro: The 36V label is looser than it sounds. Makita builds a 36V tool by running two 18V batteries in series, while other brands reach similar power on their own single-pack platforms. What matters is not the badge but how much air the tool moves and how long the batteries last, and listings are rarely upfront about either.

We reviewed eight cordless blowers, including three true 36V-class Makita and Mayoki tools, two EGO models and three 18V picks that serve as lighter alternatives. Each was ranked on airflow, weight where stated and kit contents. We note when a listing does not say it is 36V.

products.name: Makita XBU02PT 36V (18V X2) LXT Brushless Blower Kit
products.verdict: A complete 36V kit with batteries and charger, 473 CFM and zero gas to manage.
products.description:
The XBU02PT is Makita's 36V (two 18V) brushless blower in a complete kit with batteries and charger included. It lists 473 CFM and zero emissions, with no gas or oil to manage.

It wins because it works out of the box, where the XBU02Z is a bare tool. It trails the EGO on raw airflow but is easier to stand behind for ordinary yards.

Buy it for a typical suburban property and a long-term battery platform. Skip it if you need the strongest air possible.
cons: Kit costs more than the bare tool
products.idealFor: Homeowners who want a ready-to-use 36V blower.

products.name: EGO Power+ Cordless Electric Leaf Blower (880 CFM)
products.verdict: Up to 880 CFM and a turbo mode reaching 200 MPH. The strongest here by far.
products.description:
This EGO Power+ listing claims up to 880 CFM, and a turbo mode reaching speeds up to 200 MPH that moves wet leaves and caked debris.

It ranks second because it is the most expensive pick and does not state that it is a 36V tool. It beats every other listing on airflow.

Buy it for big or messy jobs. Skip it if you want to stay on a Makita or Milwaukee platform.
products.idealFor: Large yards and wet, heavy debris.

products.name: Makita XBU02Z 36V (18V X2) LXT Brushless Blower
products.verdict: The tool-only XBU02Z with a 6-stage velocity dial and a 61 dB(A) sound rating.
products.description:
The XBU02Z is the bare-tool version of Makita's 36V brushless blower, with a 6-stage air velocity dial and a 61 dB(A) sound rating per the ANSI B175.2 standard.

It ranks third because you must supply batteries and a charger, which the kit includes. For a Makita owner that makes it the cheapest way in.

Buy it if you already have two 18V LXT batteries. Otherwise take the kit.
products.idealFor: Makita owners who already have batteries.

products.name: EGO POWER+ Cordless Electric Leaf Blower (530 CFM)
products.verdict: 530 CFM, suited to lighter cleanup rather than heavy wet debris.
products.description:
This EGO POWER+ listing states 530 CFM, which is enough for dry leaves and grass clippings but not the place to start with caked, soggy piles. There is no gas, oil or spark plug to look after.

It ranks below the 880 CFM model because it moves less air, and it costs far less. Against the Makita kit, it has a bit more CFM on paper.

A fit for small to mid-size lawns. Heavy leaf drifts need a stronger tool.

products.name: Mayoki Cordless Leaf Blower Compatible with Makita 18V Battery
products.verdict: A dual-battery design with 570 CFM that uses Makita 18V packs. Cheap for Makita owners.
products.description:
The Mayoki lists 570 CFM from a true dual-battery design for 36V-class output, with a mid-mounted motor and balanced center of gravity, three speeds and a Turbo mode.

It ranks fifth because it is an unbranded tool for use with Makita batteries and we cannot confirm how well it works with them. It beats the Makita kit on CFM and costs far less, without batteries.

A smart buy for Makita owners on a tight budget. Check compatibility with your packs.
products.idealFor: Makita battery owners who want cheap power.

products.name: Milwaukee M18 FUEL 120 MPH 450 CFM 18-Volt Lithium Ion Brushless
products.verdict: A single-18V brushless handheld with 450 CFM and 120 MPH. Fits the M18 ecosystem.
products.description:
The Milwaukee M18 FUEL blower lists 450 CFM, 120 MPH and a brushless motor in a handheld body, and it works with the wider M18 battery line.

It ranks sixth because it is a single 18V tool, not a 36V one, and moves a little less air than the Makita kit. It is the pick for people already on Milwaukee.

Buy it if you own M18 batteries. Otherwise, a 36V-class tool is stronger.
cons: Less airflow than the Makita kit

products.name: Makita XBU03Z 18V LXT Lithium-Ion Brushless Cordless Blower
products.verdict: A single-18V Makita with 459 CFM, an in-line fan and a speed lock.
products.description:
The XBU03Z is a single-18V Makita with 459 CFM, an in-line fan design for better balance and a speed lock for continuous operation.

It ranks seventh because it is a single 18V tool and not 36V, and the XBU02PT gives about the same CFM with more headroom. It does cost less and uses a single battery.

Buy it if you have one LXT battery and a small lawn. Step up for bigger jobs.
products.idealFor: Small lawns with a single LXT battery.

products.name: Metabo HPT 18V Cordless Compact Blower
products.verdict: A 2.6 lb compact blower at the lowest cost. Only 124 CFM, so it is for light work.
products.description:
The Metabo HPT compact blower weighs just 2.6 lbs, lists 124 CFM and belongs to the expanding MultiVolt battery ecosystem.

It ranks last because 124 CFM is a fraction of the other picks, and it is a single 18V tool. It wins on weight and price.

Buy it for decks, patios and workshop sweeps. Do not buy it for a lawn.
products.skipIf: You clear leaves from a lawn.

methodology.title: 36V-class power
methodology.description: We ranked true 36V and dual-battery tools first, and marked single-18V tools as lighter alternatives.

methodology.title: Airflow on paper
methodology.description: CFM and air speed were compared where listings state them.

methodology.title: Kit contents
methodology.description: Bare tools and kits differ in cost, so batteries and chargers were counted.

methodology.title: Platform lock-in
methodology.description: Battery platform matters over years, so compatibility with wider tool lines was weighed.

methodology.title: Value in the field
methodology.description: Each tool was weighed against its price tier relative to the other seven.

whatMatters.detail: Makita's 36V tools run two 18V batteries together. Other brands use their own single-pack platforms. Do not compare voltage alone; compare stated CFM and runtime. Look for the words 18V x2 or dual battery on the listing.

whatMatters.factor: Check what is in the box
whatMatters.detail: Makita sells the same blower as a bare tool and as a kit with batteries and a charger. For a new buyer, the kit is almost always cheaper than buying batteries separately. Read the box contents on the page before ordering.

The battery is the expensive part. Choose a platform whose other tools you might buy, such as Makita LXT, Milwaukee M18, EGO or Metabo HPT MultiVolt. A cheaper tool on the wrong platform can cost more over time.
CFM is volume and MPH is speed. Wet leaves need speed, large piles need volume. Check both on the listing, and be careful with listings that give neither, as the Makita XBU02Z does.

A blower with batteries on board gets heavy. Mid-mounted motors and in-line fans improve balance, and lighter tools like the Metabo HPT save your arm. Choose weight carefully if your sessions run longer than 20 minutes.

faq.a: Two 18V batteries run together in one tool to make 36V. Makita uses this setup on the XBU02Z and XBU02PT.

faq.q: Do I need to buy batteries separately?
faq.a: For the Makita XBU02Z and the Mayoki, yes. The Makita XBU02PT kit includes batteries and a charger.
The listing does not state it. EGO uses its own battery platform.

faq.q: Is a single-18V blower strong enough for leaves?
faq.a: For small lawns, yes. The Milwaukee M18 lists 450 CFM, though 36V class tools have more headroom.

faq.q: Will the Mayoki work with my Makita batteries?
faq.a: It is sold as compatible with Makita 18V packs, but it is not a Makita product. Confirm with the seller.

faq.q: How loud is the Makita XBU02Z?
faq.a: The listing states 61 dB(A) per ANSI B175.2. That figure comes from the listing, not our own measurement.

finalTake: For most buyers the Makita XBU02PT kit is the right answer: a 36V brushless tool with batteries and a charger included. For raw force, the EGO Power+ 880 CFM listing is the strongest. If you already own Makita batteries, the bare XBU02Z saves money. Pick an 18V model only for small jobs, and read each listing for what it actually includes.
